newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Fischler says EU grain output rise "alarming".
newsitem.headline: Fischler says EU grain output rise "alarming".

text.p: European Union Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler said on Wednesday that EU grain production was increasing at an "alarming" rate.
EU grain output is estimated at a record of some 202 million tonnes in 1996, around 27 million tonnes higher than in 1995.
"(Lower set-aside) coupled with the annual increase in average yields is alarming. The Commission feels that this will probably increase by 10 percent," Fischler told a news conference.

"This means the cereals quantities will increase by some 25 percent in two years (1996/97, 1997/98). That's a huge increase," he said, adding that was why a seven percent cut in cereals area aids was proposed.
But he said it was too early to propose a set-aside rate for 1997/98 until there was a clearer picture of this year's harvest.
"It's very difficult to say at this stage what set-aside should be for next season," he said.
"We must wait for a firm estimate," he added, declining to say when a proposal would be made.
The EU last summer halved the cereals set-aside rate to five percent for the 1997 harvest after public stocks fell to the lowest level for many years and prices soared.
"My objective is to ensure that new grain mountains are not formed," Fischler said in reply to a question.
He said that a choice would have to be made between two alternatives: either set-aside rates are increased or export refunds are removed.

Otherwise the EU would run into GATT limits on subsidised grain exports, he warned. But he added that the problem would not occur immediately because the EU was able to export without subsidies last season after world prices rose above EU levels.

"One thing is clear. At the end of the current GATT period towards the end of the century...we are going to come up against this limit," he said, adding that cereals reforms would have to be considered when the set-aside rate is set for next season.
Fischler added that the impact of 1992 price-cutting reforms will also have bottomed out by the end of the decade.
Cereals and oilseed policy will have to be reviewed to prepare for the next round of world farm trade talks starting in 1999 and the EU's expansion eastwards early next century, he said.
"A policy such as the CAP (Common Agricultural Policy)...cannot stand still," he said in a statement.

To help prepare for the reforms, by the end of March the Commission is due to complete a detailed analysis of domestic and international cereals production and market trends over the next five to 10 years.
